issues.legal_issue: A charge may be quashed in the exercise of inherent jurisdiction when the record provides strong reasons to find that no material connects the accused to the alleged offence.
material_facts: The prosecution relied principally on intercepted calls between a private intermediary and other officials, and between the intermediary and the accused official.
One call did not implicate the accused in the alleged settlement; another used ambiguous, cryptic expressions that could not reliably be connected to the raid or an agreed bribe.
The other material, including evidence of contact between the intermediary and the accused, did not establish that the intermediary had apprised the accused of developments concerning the raid.
The High Court quashed the framed charges, and the appeal challenged that order.
issues.conclusion: The High Court acted within its powers in quashing the charges because the record contained no material connecting the accused to the offence; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: At the charge-framing stage, a court considers the record and accompanying documents to determine whether there is ground to presume that an offence was committed, without conducting a detailed assessment of evidentiary sufficiency. A court considering a request under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash a framed charge should interfere only for strong reasons, in exceptional cases and to serve the interests of justice or prevent abuse of process. The court must be satisfied that the facts and ingredients of an offence are present, even though the required showing may be less than a prima facie case.

predicates.appeal_from_quashing_framed_charge: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an order that quashed charges already framed against an accused.
predicates.ambiguous_key_evidence: The principal evidence relied on to connect the accused to the alleged offence consists of communications whose meaning or connection to the alleged conduct is unclear.
predicates.no_material_linking_accused: The remaining record does not materially connect the accused to the alleged offence.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges the quashing of framed charges, unclear principal evidence and the absence of other material connecting the accused support upholding the quashing.

issues.legal_issue: A criminal conspiracy charge requires evidence capable of establishing an agreement to commit an illegal act or to do a lawful act by illegal means.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that the accused official participated in a plan involving a raid and the extraction of illegal gratification through a private intermediary.
The call said to convey the successful completion of the alleged plan was ambiguous and could not reliably be connected to the raid or a bribe agreement.
The other relied-on call indicated that the accused was not involved in the discussion about the raid and alleged settlement.
The Court found no direct or circumstantial evidence establishing the accused’s knowledge of or agreement to the alleged conspiracy.
issues.conclusion: There was no material evidence to bring home the conspiracy charge against the accused.
issues.legal_principle: A conspiracy requires an agreement between two or more persons to do an illegal act or to do an act that is not illegal by illegal means. Under Central Bureau of Investigation, Hyderabad v. K. Narayana Rao, (2012) 9 SCC 512, an agreement may be proved by direct or circumstantial evidence, but proved circumstances must support the inference of agreement and be incapable of another reasonable explanation; suspicion and surmise are insufficient.

predicates.prosecution_for_conspiracy: The proceeding includes a charge that the accused agreed with another person to commit an illegal act or to use illegal means.
predicates.no_evidence_of_agreement: The prosecution has no direct or circumstantial evidence that the accused agreed to the alleged criminal plan.
predicates.circumstances_allow_other_reasonable_exp: The circumstances relied on by the prosecution are reasonably capable of an explanation other than the accused’s participation in the alleged agreement.

issues.definition: In a conspiracy prosecution, an unsupported agreement and circumstances with another reasonable explanation mean that the conspiracy charge is not supported.

issues.legal_issue: A charge for obtaining illegal gratification under the relevant corruption offences cannot stand without evidence of a demand for the gratification.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that gratification was negotiated and collected through a private intermediary in connection with an official raid.
The evidence did not establish that the accused demanded or agreed to demand illegal gratification, or that the accused accepted or obtained it.
The intercepted calls relied on by the prosecution did not reliably connect the accused to the alleged demand or settlement.
issues.conclusion: There was no evidence that the accused demanded or accepted illegal gratification, and the prosecution material did not support the charge against the accused.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 7 and 13(1)(d)(i) and (ii) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, proof of demand is indispensable; mere possession, recovery or acceptance of money without proof of demand is insufficient. P. Satyanarayana Murthy v. District Inspector of Police, State of A.P., (2015) 10 SCC 152, applying B. Jayaraj, also holds that the presumption under Section 20 applies only to an offence under Section 7 and depends on proof of acceptance, which in turn requires proof of demand.

predicates.prosecution_for_illegal_gratification: The proceeding includes a charge that the accused sought, accepted or obtained illegal gratification.
predicates.no_evidence_of_demand: The prosecution evidence does not establish that the accused demanded illegal gratification.

issues.definition: In a prosecution for illegal gratification, the absence of evidence of demand means that the charge is unsupported.
